title: What is a DBMS? Discuss its advantages over a traditional file-processing system.
answer_html:
Definition

A Database Management System (DBMS) is software that interacts with end-users, applications, and the database itself to capture and analyze data. It allows users to create, read, update, and delete data in a database.

Advantages over File-Processing
  • Data Redundancy and Inconsistency: Centralizes data, eliminating duplicate files and ensuring updates propagate everywhere.
  • Data Isolation: Applications do not need to know the physical structure of the data files.
  • Integrity Problems: Allows defining explicit integrity constraints (e.g., account balance > 0).
  • Security Problems: Offers fine-grained access control and user authorization.
  • Concurrent Access: Manages simultaneous access securely, preventing anomalies.
simplified_html:
Quick Recall:

  • Data Redundancy and Inconsistency: Centralizes data, eliminating duplicate files and ensuring updates propagate everywhere.
  • Data Isolation: Applications do not need to know the physical structure of the data files.
  • Integrity Problems: Allows defining explicit integrity constraints (e.g., account balance > 0).

title: What do you mean by data redundancy and data inconsistency? How does a DBMS take care of these problems?
answer_html:
Definitions
  • Data Redundancy: The unnecessary duplication of data in a database. (e.g., storing a student's address in both the Library and Department files).
  • Data Inconsistency: A consequence of redundancy where different copies of the same data hold different values (e.g., address updated in Library but not Department).
DBMS Solution

A DBMS minimizes redundancy by storing a single, centralized copy of the data (Data Normalization). Because there is only one authoritative copy, inconsistency is inherently prevented.

  • Data Inconsistency: A consequence of redundancy where different copies of the same data hold different values (e.g., address updated in Library but not Department).

  • Data Independence: DB systems separate applications from data structure; File systems tightly couple applications to file formats.
  • Querying: DB systems provide robust query languages (SQL); File systems require custom application code to extract data.

title: Draw and explain the three-level (ANSI-SPARC) architecture of a DBMS.
answer_html:
The Three Levels
  1. External Level (View Level): The highest level, describing only the part of the database relevant to a specific user group (hiding the rest).
  2. Conceptual Level (Logical Level): Describes what data is stored in the entire database and the relationships among those data. Used by DBAs.
  3. Internal Level (Physical Level): Describes exactly how the data is physically stored on disk (data structures, file organizations).
Exam Tip: The primary objective of this architecture is to achieve Data Independence.

  • Internal Level (Physical Level): Describes exactly how the data is physically stored on disk (data structures, file organizations).

title: What is data abstraction? Discuss the three levels of data abstraction used in a DBMS.
answer_html:
Definition

Data abstraction is the process of hiding complex internal data structures and storage details from the user, presenting only a simplified, usable view of the data.

Three Levels
  • Physical Level: Hides the complexity of block structures, indexing, and bytes on disk.
  • Logical Level: Hides physical storage but reveals entities, data types, and relationships. Developers interact here.
  • View Level: Hides the entire logical schema except for specific fields the end-user is authorized to see (e.g., a teller seeing only names and balances).

title: Define the terms schema and instance. Why is this distinction important?

  • Instance: The snapshot of data residing in the database at a specific moment in time. It changes frequently.
Importance

title: What is data independence? Explain logical and physical data independence with a suitable example.
answer_html:
Definition

Data independence is the ability to modify a schema definition in one level without affecting a schema definition in the next higher level.

Types
  • Physical Data Independence: Ability to modify the internal/physical schema without altering the conceptual schema. Example: Changing a file from sequential to a B+ tree index to improve performance; application code doesn't change.
  • Logical Data Independence: Ability to modify the conceptual schema without altering the external schema (user views). Example: Splitting an Employee table into two normalized tables; the original view can be maintained using a SQL JOIN, shielding the frontend application.

title: Compare the hierarchical, network, relational and object-oriented data models. Which one is most widely used today and why?
answer_html:
Comparison
  • Hierarchical: Data organized in a tree structure (1:N relationships). Fast but inflexible; requires navigating rigid pointers.
  • Network: Data organized in a graph (M:N relationships allowed). Highly complex and difficult to maintain.
  • Relational: Data organized in 2D tables (relations). Uses declarative SQL. Extremely flexible and mathematically sound.
  • Object-Oriented: Data stored as objects with methods, matching OOP languages. Best for complex data (e.g., CAD/CAM).
Most Widely Used

The Relational Model is most widely used today due to its simplicity, robust theoretical foundation (normalization), and standard interface (SQL) which provides unparalleled data independence.

title: Explain the terms super key, candidate key, primary key and foreign key with a suitable example.
answer_html:
Explanation
  • Super Key: Any combination of columns that uniquely identifies a row. (e.g., StudentID + Name)
  • Candidate Key: A minimal super key; it uniquely identifies a row with no unnecessary columns. (e.g., StudentID or Email)
  • Primary Key: The specific candidate key chosen to identify rows. Cannot be NULL. (e.g., StudentID)
  • Foreign Key: A column that refers to the primary key of another table, enforcing referential integrity. (e.g., Dept_ID in a Student table referencing the Department table)

title: What are integrity constraints in a relational model? Explain domain, key, entity and referential integrity.
answer_html:
Definition

Integrity constraints are rules applied to a database to ensure the data is accurate, consistent, and valid.

The Four Constraints
  • Domain Constraint: Restricts the values a column can hold to a valid set (e.g., Age must be a positive integer).
  • Key Constraint: Ensures that candidate/primary keys are completely unique for every row.
  • Entity Integrity: States that no part of a Primary Key can be NULL, because a NULL value cannot uniquely identify a row.
  • Referential Integrity: States that if a foreign key exists in a relation, its value must either match a primary key value in the referenced relation or be NULL. (e.g., You cannot enroll a student in a non-existent Course_ID).

Quick Recall:

title: Explain generalization and specialization in the Extended E-R model with an example of each.
answer_html:
Specialization (Top-Down)

The process of defining a set of subclasses from a single entity type (the superclass). It involves identifying characteristics that distinguish some entities in the set from others.
Example: An Employee superclass can be specialized into Engineer, Manager, and Technician subclasses based on job role.

Generalization (Bottom-Up)

The reverse process of specialization. Multiple entity types with common attributes are synthesized into a single, generalized superclass.
Example: Car and Truck entities share attributes like Vehicle_ID and Price, so they can be generalized into a Vehicle superclass.

  • It involves identifying characteristics that distinguish some entities in the set from others.

title: What is the difference between overlapping and disjoint specialization? Illustrate with an example.
answer_html:
Disjoint Specialization

An entity can be a member of at most one subclass of the specialization. Denoted by a 'd' in the circle.
Example: An Employee can be either an Hourly_Employee or a Salaried_Employee, but never both at the same time.

Overlapping Specialization

An entity may be a member of more than one subclass of the specialization. Denoted by an 'o' in the circle.
Example: A Person can simultaneously be an Alumnus and an Employee of a university.

title: What is aggregation in E-R modelling? When is it required? Explain with an example.
answer_html:
Definition

Aggregation is an abstraction where a relationship set (and its associated entities) is treated as a higher-level entity set.

When is it required?

The basic E-R model cannot express relationships among relationships. Aggregation is required when a relationship between two entities needs to participate in another relationship with a third entity.

Example

Consider Employee working on a Project. This forms the relationship Works_On. If we want to record the Manager who oversees this specific (Employee-Project) assignment, we aggregate Works_On into a single entity, and create a new relationship Manages between it and Manager.
simplified_html:
Quick Recall:

  • Aggregation is an abstraction where a relationship set (and its associated entities) is treated as a higher-level entity set.
  • The basic E-R model cannot express relationships among relationships.

  • Many-to-One (N:1): An entity in A is associated with at most one entity in B. An entity in B is associated with any number of entities in A.
  • Many-to-Many (M:N): An entity in A is associated with any number of entities in B, and vice versa.

title: What is a functional dependency? Why is it important in the process of database design?
answer_html:
Definition

A functional dependency (FD) is a constraint between two sets of attributes in a relation. If A → B (A determines B), then for every valid instance of the relation, any two tuples that agree on the attribute A must also agree on the attribute B.

Importance

Functional dependencies are the theoretical bedrock of Normalization. They are used to specify constraints on data, discover candidate keys, and decompose relations to eliminate redundancy and update anomalies.

Quick Recall:

  • A functional dependency (FD) is a constraint between two sets of attributes in a relation.
  • If A → B (A determines B), then for every valid instance of the relation, any two tuples that agree on the attribute A must also agree on the attribute B.

title: What are insertion, deletion and update anomalies? How does normalization help remove them?
answer_html:
The Three Anomalies
  • Update Anomaly: If data is stored redundantly, changing it in one row requires changing it in all rows. Missing one causes inconsistency (e.g., changing a department's location).
  • Insertion Anomaly: The inability to add data to the database due to absence of other data (e.g., unable to add a new Department because it has no Employees yet, and Employee_ID is the primary key).
  • Deletion Anomaly: The unintended loss of data when deleting a row (e.g., deleting the only employee in a department also deletes the department's information).
How Normalization Helps

Normalization resolves these by decomposing large, poorly structured tables into smaller, well-structured tables where each table represents a single logical theme or entity. By linking them with foreign keys, redundancy is eliminated, which inherently solves update, insertion, and deletion anomalies.

  • Deletion Anomaly: The unintended loss of data when deleting a row (e.g., deleting the only employee in a department also deletes the department's information).

title: What is normalization? Explain 1NF, 2NF and 3NF with a suitable example.
answer_html:
Definition

Normalization is the process of organizing data to minimize redundancy and eliminate anomalies by dividing larger tables into smaller tables and defining relationships between them using functional dependencies.

The Normal Forms
  • First Normal Form (1NF): All attributes must be atomic (indivisible). No repeating groups or arrays allowed in a cell.
  • Second Normal Form (2NF): Must be in 1NF, and all non-key attributes must be fully functionally dependent on the entire primary key. (Eliminates partial dependencies).
  • Third Normal Form (3NF): Must be in 2NF, and no non-key attribute can be dependent on another non-key attribute. (Eliminates transitive dependencies: X → Y and Y → Z).
simplified_html:
Quick Recall:

  • First Normal Form (1NF): All attributes must be atomic (indivisible). No repeating groups or arrays allowed in a cell.
  • Second Normal Form (2NF): Must be in 1NF, and all non-key attributes must be fully functionally dependent on the entire primary key. (Eliminates partial dependencies).
  • Third Normal Form (3NF): Must be in 2NF, and no non-key attribute can be dependent on another non-key attribute. (Eliminates transitive dependencies: X → Y and Y → Z).

title: Define BCNF. How is it different from 3NF? Support your answer with an example.
answer_html:
Definition

Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) requires that for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y, X must be a super key. It is a stronger, stricter version of 3NF.

Difference from 3NF

3NF allows a dependency X → Y where X is NOT a super key, provided that Y is a prime attribute (part of a candidate key). BCNF does not allow this exception. A table can be in 3NF but fail BCNF if it has overlapping candidate keys.

Example

Consider Relation(Student, Course, Instructor). Keys are (Student, Course) and (Student, Instructor). FD: Instructor → Course.
It is in 3NF because Course is a prime attribute. However, it violates BCNF because Instructor is not a super key.
simplified_html:
Quick Recall:

  • Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) requires that for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y, X must be a super key.
  • It is a stronger, stricter version of 3NF.

title: Write a short note on 4NF and 5NF, with an example of each.
answer_html:
Fourth Normal Form (4NF)

Deals with Multi-valued Dependencies (MVD). A table is in 4NF if it is in BCNF and contains no non-trivial multi-valued dependencies (where one attribute determines a set of values for another, independent of a third).
Example: An Employee has multiple Skills and multiple Dependents. Storing them in one table creates massive redundancy. We split into (Emp, Skill) and (Emp, Dependent).

Fifth Normal Form (5NF)

Deals with Join Dependencies. Also known as Project-Join Normal Form (PJNF). A table is in 5NF if it is in 4NF and cannot be decomposed into smaller tables without losing data (lossless join). It ensures that all join dependencies are implied by candidate keys.
simplified_html:
Quick Recall:

  • Deals with Multi-valued Dependencies (MVD).
  • A table is in 4NF if it is in BCNF and contains no non-trivial multi-valued dependencies (where one attribute determines a set of values for another, independent of a third).

title: What is lossless-join decomposition? Explain with an example.
answer_html:
Definition

Lossless-join decomposition means that if a relation R is decomposed into R1 and R2, joining them back together via a Natural Join will yield the exact original relation R, without any missing rows (loss of data) or extra spurious rows (creation of invalid data).

Condition

The decomposition is lossless if the common attribute(s) between R1 and R2 form a super key for either R1 or R2. (i.e., R1 ∩ R2 → R1 OR R1 ∩ R2 → R2).

Example

Splitting Employee(ID, Name, Dept, Dept_Location) into Emp(ID, Name, Dept) and Department(Dept, Dept_Location) is lossless because their intersection, Dept, is a primary key for the Department table.
simplified_html:
Quick Recall:

  • Lossless-join decomposition means that if a relation R is decomposed into R1 and R2, joining them back together via a Natural Join will yield the exact original relation R, without any missing rows (loss of data) or...
  • The decomposition is lossless if the common attribute(s) between R1 and R2 form a super key for either R1 or R2.

title: Define dependency-preserving decomposition and give a suitable example.
answer_html:
Definition

A decomposition is dependency-preserving if the union of the functional dependencies in the decomposed relations logically implies all the functional dependencies of the original relation. This ensures that updates can be checked for validity without joining the tables back together.

Example

Original Relation: R(A, B, C)
Functional Dependencies (FDs): A → B, B → C
Decomposition: R1(A, B) and R2(B, C).
FDs in R1: A → B.
FDs in R2: B → C.
Since (A → B) ∪ (B → C) covers all original FDs, it is a dependency-preserving decomposition.
simplified_html:
Quick Recall:

  • A decomposition is dependency-preserving if the union of the functional dependencies in the decomposed relations logically implies all the functional dependencies of the original relation.
  • This ensures that updates can be checked for validity without joining the tables back together.

title: Given a relation R(A, B, C, D, E) with the functional dependency set F = {A -> B, BC -> D, D -> E}, compute the closure of {A, C} and state whether {A, C} is a candidate key of R.
answer_html:
Computing {A, C}+
  1. Start with the base set: {A, C}
  2. Using A → B, add B. The set becomes {A, B, C}
  3. Using BC → D (we have both B and C), add D. The set becomes {A, B, C, D}
  4. Using D → E, add E. The set becomes {A, B, C, D, E}
Conclusion

Since the closure of {A, C} contains all the attributes of the relation R, {A, C} is a super key. Assuming no proper subset of {A, C} can determine all attributes, {A, C} is a Candidate Key.

  • Using BC → D (we have both B and C), add D. The set becomes {A, B, C, D}

title: Given a relation R(A, B, C, D) with the functional dependency set F = {AB -> C, C -> D, D -> A}, find all the candidate keys of R and state the highest normal form it satisfies.
answer_html:

  • {B, C}+ = {A, B, C, D} (since C → D and D → A)
  • {B, D}+ = {A, B, C, D} (since D → A and AB → C)

The candidate keys are AB, BC, and BD. All attributes are prime attributes except none (every attribute is part of at least one candidate key).

Highest Normal Form

Because there are no non-prime attributes, the relation is automatically in 3NF.

title: Explain generalization, specialization and aggregation in the Extended E-R model.
answer_html:
Specialization (Top-Down)

The process of defining a set of subclasses from an entity type based on distinguishing characteristics.
Example: An Employee can be specialized into Hourly_Emp and Salaried_Emp.

Generalization (Bottom-Up)

The reverse of specialization. Extracting shared characteristics from multiple entity types to create a generalized superclass.
Example: Car and Truck generalized into Vehicle.

Aggregation

Treating a relationship between entities as a single abstract entity, allowing relationships to participate in other relationships.
Example: A Project and Employee have a Works_On relationship. A Manager manages the entire Works_On relationship, treating it as one aggregated entity.

title: What is decomposition? Explain the concepts of lossless-join and dependency-preserving decomposition.
answer_html:
Decomposition is the process of breaking down a large, poorly-designed relation into two or more smaller relations to eliminate redundancy and anomalies.

Lossless-Join Decomposition

A decomposition of R into R1 and R2 is lossless if joining R1 and R2 back together using a Natural Join yields the exact original relation R, without generating spurious (fake) tuples.

Condition: The common attributes must be a candidate key for at least one of the decomposed relations (i.e., R1 ∩ R2 → R1 or R1 ∩ R2 → R2).

Dependency-Preserving Decomposition

A decomposition is dependency-preserving if all original functional dependencies can be checked and enforced using only the decomposed relations, without needing to join them back together.

Quick Recall:

  • Decomposition is the process of breaking down a large, poorly-designed relation into two or more smaller relations to eliminate redundancy and anomalies.
  • A decomposition of R into R1 and R2 is lossless if joining R1 and R2 back together using a Natural Join yields the exact original relation R, without generating spurious (fake) tuples.

title: How is decomposition related to normalization? Explain with a small example.
answer_html:
Normalization uses Decomposition as its primary mechanism. When a relation violates a normal form, we decompose it into smaller relations that satisfy the normal form.

Example

Suppose a relation R(EmpID, EmpName, DeptID, DeptName) where EmpID → EmpName, DeptID and DeptID → DeptName.

  • This violates 3NF due to the transitive dependency (EmpID → DeptID → DeptName).
  • Normalization Process: We decompose R into two relations to remove the redundancy:
    1. Employee(EmpID, EmpName, DeptID)
    2. Department(DeptID, DeptName)

This decomposition is both lossless-join (because DeptID is a primary key in Department) and dependency-preserving.

title: What is a transaction? Explain the ACID properties with the help of a bank transfer example.
answer_html:
A transaction is a logical unit of work consisting of one or more SQL statements that must be executed entirely or not at all.

ACID Properties (Bank Transfer Example: A to B):

  • Atomicity: "All or nothing." If money is deducted from A, it MUST be credited to B. If either fails, the entire transaction is rolled back.
  • Consistency: The database must remain in a valid state. The total sum of A + B's balances must be the same before and after the transaction.
  • Isolation: Concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other. If another transaction reads A's balance during the transfer, it will see the state either strictly before or strictly after, not midway.
  • Durability: Once the transaction is committed, the changes are permanent and will survive system crashes.

Transaction State Diagram
simplified_html:
Quick Recall:

  • Atomicity: "All or nothing." If money is deducted from A, it MUST be credited to B. If either fails, the entire transaction is rolled back.
  • Consistency: The database must remain in a valid state. The total sum of A + B's balances must be the same before and after the transaction.
  • Isolation: Concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other. If another transaction reads A's balance during the transfer, it will see the state either strictly before or strictly after, not midway.

title: Explain COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT with a suitable example on the ACCOUNT table.
answer_html:
• COMMIT: Saves all changes made during the current transaction permanently.
  • ROLLBACK: Undoes all changes made during the current transaction, reverting to the last commit.
  • SAVEPOINT: Sets a marker within a transaction so you can roll back to that specific point without canceling the entire transaction.
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance - 500 WHERE Acc_No = 'A101';
SAVEPOINT step1;
UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance + 500 WHERE Acc_No = 'A102';
-- If something goes wrong here:
ROLLBACK TO step1; -- Undoes only the A102 update
COMMIT; -- Saves the final state
simplified_html:
Quick Recall:

  • COMMIT: Saves all changes made during the current transaction permanently.
  • ROLLBACK: Undoes all changes made during the current transaction, reverting to the last commit.
  • SAVEPOINT: Sets a marker within a transaction so you can roll back to that specific point without canceling the entire transaction.

title: Write a transaction that transfers Rs. 3000 from account A102 to account A103, placing a SAVEPOINT just before the transfer, and finally commit it.
answer_html:
START TRANSACTION;
SAVEPOINT before_transfer;

UPDATE ACCOUNT 
SET Balance = Balance - 3000 
WHERE Acc_No = 'A102';

SET Balance = Balance + 3000 
WHERE Acc_No = 'A103';

title: Using a searched CASE statement, classify each account's Balance as 'High' if it is 25000 or more, 'Medium' if it is 15000 or more, and 'Low' otherwise.
answer_html:
SELECT Acc_No, Name, Balance,

    END AS Balance_Category

title: In one or two lines each, state the purpose of a stored procedure, a sequence (AUTO_INCREMENT in MySQL), a cursor and a trigger.
answer_html:
• Stored Procedure: A pre-compiled collection of SQL statements saved in the database that can be executed as a single callable routine.
  • Sequence (AUTO_INCREMENT): Automatically generates unique, sequential numeric values, typically used for primary keys.
  • Cursor: A database object used to retrieve and process rows one by one from a result set inside a stored procedure.
  • Trigger: A special type of stored procedure that automatically executes (fires) in response to specific DML events (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) on a table.
simplified_html:
Quick Recall:

  • Stored Procedure: A pre-compiled collection of SQL statements saved in the database that can be executed as a single callable routine.
  • Sequence (AUTO_INCREMENT): Automatically generates unique, sequential numeric values, typically used for primary keys.
  • Cursor: A database object used to retrieve and process rows one by one from a result set inside a stored procedure.

title: What is the difference between a BEFORE trigger and an AFTER trigger? What do the keywords NEW and OLD refer to inside a trigger?
answer_html:
BEFORE Trigger executes before the triggering DML operation is applied (useful for validation/modification of incoming data). AFTER Trigger executes after the operation (useful for auditing or cascading changes to other tables).

NEW refers to the incoming data (being inserted or updated). OLD refers to the existing data in the table before the operation (being updated or deleted).

Quick Recall:

  • BEFORE Trigger executes before the triggering DML operation is applied (useful for validation/modification of incoming data).
  • AFTER Trigger executes after the operation (useful for auditing or cascading changes to other tables).

title: What is the purpose of exception handling in a stored procedure? Briefly explain DECLARE ... HANDLER and the SIGNAL statement.
answer_html:
Exception handling ensures that if an error occurs during execution, the stored procedure can catch it and gracefully handle it (e.g., rolling back a transaction) instead of crashing.

  • DECLARE ... HANDLER: Defines a block of code to execute when a specific error or condition occurs (e.g., DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION).
  • SIGNAL: Used to artificially raise a custom error or exception, returning a custom SQLSTATE and message to the caller.
simplified_html:
Quick Recall:

  • DECLARE ... HANDLER: Defines a block of code to execute when a specific error or condition occurs (e.g., DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION).
  • SIGNAL: Used to artificially raise a custom error or exception, returning a custom SQLSTATE and message to the caller.

title: Define a transaction. Mention the two ways in which a transaction can terminate.
answer_html:
A transaction is a logical unit of database processing that includes one or more operations (such as read, write, or update). It executes as an indivisible unit to preserve database consistency.

A transaction terminates in two ways:

  • Commit: The transaction completes successfully, making all its modifications permanent and durable on disk.
  • Abort (Rollback): The transaction terminates abnormally; all partial changes are undone, returning the database to its pre-transaction state.
simplified_html: Think of a transaction as an all-or-nothing contract (like transferring ₹500: both deducting from account A and adding to account B must succeed). If everything goes well, it commits (saved forever). If something breaks midway, it aborts (undone, money never leaves).

title: Three transactions are running such that T1 waits for a lock held by T2, T2 waits for a lock held by T3, and T3 waits for a lock held by T1. Draw the wait-for graph and state whether a deadlock exists.
answer_html:
A Wait-For Graph (WFG) is a directed graph where vertices represent active transactions and directed edge $T_i \to T_j$ indicates that $T_i$ is waiting for a lock held by $T_j$.

Deadlock Status: Yes, a deadlock exists. The wait-for graph contains the directed cycle $T_1 \to T_2 \to T_3 \to T_1$. In concurrency control, a directed cycle in a WFG is a necessary and sufficient condition for deadlock.
simplified_html: T1 is waiting for T2, T2 is waiting for T3, and T3 is waiting for T1. This creates a circular waiting loop where nobody can move forward. A cycle in the Wait-For Graph always means a deadlock.

title: What is meant by a recoverable schedule?
answer_html:
A schedule $S$ is recoverable if, for every pair of transactions $T_i$ and $T_j$ where $T_j$ reads a data item previously written by $T_i$, the commit operation of $T_i$ precedes the commit operation of $T_j$ ($Commit(T_i) < Commit(T_j)$).

  • Significance: Prevents dirty read commits. If $T_i$ aborts, $T_j$ can also be safely rolled back because it has not yet committed.
  • Database Invariant: Commercial DBMSs mandate recoverable schedules to guarantee atomicity and durability during crashes.
simplified_html: If you copy answers from a friend, you shouldn't submit your exam paper before your friend does. If your friend rips up their paper (aborts), you must be able to cancel yours too. A schedule is recoverable if the writer commits before the reader commits.

title: Define deadlock and state any two conditions that are necessary for it to occur.
answer_html:
A deadlock is an execution state where two or more concurrent transactions are permanently blocked because each holds a lock on a data item that another requires, and none can proceed without releasing locks.

Two necessary conditions for deadlock are:

  • Mutual Exclusion: A resource is held in an exclusive, non-shareable mode (such as an $X$-lock).
  • Hold and Wait: A transaction holds granted resources while requesting additional resources held by other transactions.
simplified_html: A deadlock is a complete traffic gridlock in the database: Transaction A is holding Item 1 waiting for Item 2, while Transaction B is holding Item 2 waiting for Item 1. Neither can finish without the other letting go.

title: What is a checkpoint in a DBMS? State its purpose in recovery.
answer_html:
A checkpoint is a synchronization record written to the log during normal operation after flushing all modified buffer blocks (dirty pages) from volatile memory to stable disk storage.

Purpose in recovery:

  • Bounds Log Scan: Limits how far back the recovery manager must scan the log during crash restart, eliminating the need to process the log from the very beginning.
  • Reduces Redo Work: Transactions committed prior to the checkpoint already have their updates safely on disk, significantly shortening system recovery downtime.
simplified_html: A checkpoint is like an autosave point in a video game. Instead of replaying the game from level 1 when it crashes, the DBMS only needs to restore changes made after the last checkpoint.

title: Differentiate between clustered and non-clustered indexes.
answer_html:
The key differences between clustered and non-clustered indexes are:

  • Physical Ordering: A clustered index dictates the physical sorting order of actual table rows on disk (only one clustered index per table). A non-clustered index maintains an independent logical order without rearranging physical rows.
  • Leaf Node Content: Leaf nodes of a clustered index contain the actual data records. In a non-clustered index, leaf nodes contain index keys and row pointers (RID / primary key) to data records.
simplified_html: A clustered index is like a dictionary where words are physically arranged in alphabetical order. A non-clustered index is like the index at the back of a textbook: it lists topics and tells you which page to flip to.

title: What is a fact table and a dimension table in a data warehouse?
answer_html:
In data warehouse dimensional modeling (e.g., star schema):

  • Fact Table: The central table containing quantitative numerical measurements (metrics) of a business process (e.g., units_sold, total_amount) along with foreign keys referencing related dimension tables.
  • Dimension Table: Surrounding companion tables containing descriptive contextual attributes (e.g., customer names, store locations, calendar quarters) used for filtering, grouping, and slicing analytical queries.
simplified_html: In a sales warehouse, the Fact table stores the actual numbers (sales amount, quantity). The Dimension tables store who bought it, when they bought it, and in which store (Customer, Time, Store details).

title: Draw the state diagram of a transaction and explain each of its states.
answer_html:
During its lifecycle, a database transaction progresses through several distinct execution states to guarantee ACID properties and system consistency:

  • Active: The initial execution state where the transaction begins and executes its read and write database operations.
  • Partially Committed: Entered immediately after the final statement has executed, but updates still reside in memory buffers and have not yet been flushed to stable disk storage.
  • Failed: Entered when normal execution cannot proceed due to hardware failures, logical errors, or concurrency violations.
  • Aborted: The transaction is rolled back, all dirty updates are undone, and the database is restored to its pre-transaction state. The transaction can either restart or terminate.
  • Committed: Entered when all log records and updates are permanently recorded on stable storage, guaranteeing durability.
simplified_html: A transaction starts Active. When code finishes, it is Partially Committed until written to disk, then Committed. If an error occurs anywhere, it goes to Failed and gets Aborted (rolled back).

title: Explain consistent and inconsistent states of a database using the example of a money transfer between two bank accounts that fails midway.
answer_html:
A consistent state satisfies all integrity constraints and business rules, while an inconsistent state violates these rules due to partial execution or unhandled failures.

Bank Transfer Scenario: Consider transferring ₹1,000 from Account $A$ (initial balance ₹5,000) to Account $B$ (initial balance ₹3,000). The database consistency invariant requires that total balance $A + B = ₹8,000$.

  • Midway Failure: The transaction executes A = A - 1000 ($A$ becomes ₹4,000). Before B = B + 1000 can execute, the system crashes.
  • Inconsistent State: If left unrecovered, $A + B = ₹4,000 + ₹3,000 = ₹7,000$. ₹1,000 has vanished, creating an inconsistent state.
  • Recovery to Consistent State: The recovery manager rolls back $A$ to ₹5,000 via transaction undo logs, re-establishing the invariant $A + B = ₹8,000$.
simplified_html: If you transfer ₹1,000 to a friend and the server crashes after taking money from you but before giving it to your friend, ₹1,000 has vanished into thin air (inconsistent state). The database must rollback the deduction to make the accounts consistent again.

title: List the different types of failures in a database system and explain how recovery from a transaction failure is carried out.
answer_html:
Database systems are subject to three fundamental classes of failures:

  • Transaction Failure: Internal logical errors (e.g., divide by zero, bad input) or system errors (e.g., deadlock abort, buffer overflow).
  • System Crash: Hardware malfunctions or operating system crashes causing volatile main memory contents to be lost without corrupting non-volatile disk storage.
  • Disk Failure: Head crashes or bad disk sectors destroying physical storage blocks.

Recovery from Transaction Failure:

When a transaction fails, the recovery manager performs an UNDO operation using the transaction log. It scans the log backwards, extracts the old values (before-images) of all modified data items, writes these original values back to the database, and appends an <abort T> log record.
simplified_html: Failures happen due to bad code/deadlocks (transaction failure), power outages (system crash), or hard drive damage (disk failure). When a transaction fails, the DBMS reads its log in reverse and undoes every change it made.

title: Explain the lost update and dirty read problems that arise when transactions execute concurrently, with an example of each.
answer_html:
Concurrency anomalies occur when transactions interleave without adequate synchronization:

  • Lost Update (Write-Write Conflict): Occurs when two transactions read the same data item and subsequently update it based on the earlier read value. The second write overwrites and obliterates the first write without incorporating its modifications.
    Example: Account balance is ₹100. $T_1$ reads 100 and computes 150. Concurrently, $T_2$ reads 100 and computes 120. $T_1$ writes 150, then $T_2$ writes 120. $T_1$'s ₹50 deposit is completely lost.
  • Dirty Read (Read-Write Conflict): Occurs when transaction $T_2$ reads a data item modified by transaction $T_1$ that has not yet committed. If $T_1$ subsequently aborts, $T_2$ has acted on transient, invalid data.
    Example: $T_1$ updates balance from ₹100 to ₹500. $T_2$ reads ₹500 and approves a purchase. $T_1$ aborts and rolls back to ₹100. $T_2$'s read was 'dirty'.
simplified_html: Lost update: Two people book the last seat at the exact same second, and the second booking overwrites the first. Dirty read: Reading someone's draft before they delete it and change their mind.

title: Distinguish between conflict serializability and view serializability with an example.
answer_html:
Serializability guarantees that concurrent schedules produce results identical to some serial execution:

  • Conflict Serializability: A schedule is conflict serializable if it can be transformed into a serial schedule by swapping non-conflicting concurrent operations. This holds if and only if its precedence (conflict) graph is acyclic. Tested efficiently in polynomial time $O(V + E)$.
  • View Serializability: A weaker, broader condition requiring identical initial reads, dependent reads, and final writes as some serial schedule. Testing view serializability is NP-complete.
  • Example: Consider schedule $S: R_1(A), W_2(A), W_1(A), W_3(A)$. Here, operations conflict in both directions ($T_1 \to T_2$ and $T_2 \to T_1$), producing a cycle in the precedence graph; thus $S$ is not conflict serializable. However, due to blind writes ($W_3(A)$ overwriting $A$), $S$ produces the exact same view as serial schedule $T_1 \to T_2 \to T_3$, making it view serializable.
simplified_html: Conflict serializability checks whether conflicting operations can be swapped without changing order (easy to test with graphs). View serializability is broader: it allows blind writes that overwrite values, matching final outputs even when conflicts exist.

title: Explain the role of the concurrency control manager and the lock manager, and describe how the lock table is used to grant or queue lock requests.
answer_html:
The concurrency control manager ensures serializability, isolation, and consistency across interleaved transactions. It delegates resource locking to the lock manager.

The lock manager maintains an in-memory hash table called the lock table, indexed by data item ID:

  • Granted List: Holds records of transactions currently granted a lock on the item, along with lock mode (Shared $S$ or Exclusive $X$).
  • Wait Queue: When a transaction requests an incompatible lock (e.g., $X$-lock while an $S$-lock is held), the request cannot be granted. The lock manager suspends the transaction and appends it to the item's FIFO wait queue.
  • Release & Grant: When a lock holder unlocks the item, the lock manager inspects the wait queue, awakens compatible waiting transactions, and updates the granted list.
simplified_html: The lock manager acts like a hotel receptionist with a key registry (lock table). If a room is free or multiple guests want to read only, keys are given out. If someone wants private access, later requests must wait in a queue.

title: Explain the role of TCL commands in controlling transactions.
answer_html:
Transaction Control Language (TCL) commands manage database transactions to ensure data integrity and ACID properties:

  • COMMIT: Permanently saves all changes made by the transaction to disk. Locks are released, and modifications become visible to other concurrent users.
  • ROLLBACK: Reverts all modifications made by an uncommitted transaction, returning the database to the state prior to transaction initiation or to a specified savepoint.
  • SAVEPOINT: Establishes intermediate checkpoints within a transaction. Allows partial rollback (e.g., ROLLBACK TO sp1) without undoing the entire transaction.
  • SET TRANSACTION: Configures isolation levels (e.g., READ COMMITTED, SERIALIZABLE) and access modes (READ ONLY vs READ WRITE) before operations begin.
simplified_html: TCL commands are the steering wheel of transactions: COMMIT saves your progress permanently, ROLLBACK is the undo button, SAVEPOINT lets you undo halfway, and SET TRANSACTION sets rules like read-only.

title: With an example, explain the ACID properties of a transaction.
answer_html:
ACID properties guarantee reliable database transactions. Consider transferring ₹1,000 from account $A$ to account $B$:

  • Atomicity: All operations succeed or none do. Either both debiting $A$ and crediting $B$ succeed, or the transaction aborts and leaves both balances unchanged.
  • Consistency: The transaction transforms the database from one valid state to another, preserving integrity invariants (e.g., total funds $A + B$ remains constant before and after).
  • Isolation: Intermediate states are hidden from concurrent transactions. Another transaction reading $A$ and $B$ cannot see $A$ deducted before $B$ is credited.
  • Durability: Once committed, updates persist permanently on non-volatile storage, even if a power failure or system crash occurs immediately afterward.
simplified_html: Atomicity = All or nothing. Consistency = Total money stays correct. Isolation = No one sees your transfer halfway done. Durability = Once confirmed, power cuts cannot erase the transfer.

title: Consider the schedule S: R1(A), W1(A), R2(A), W2(A), R1(B), W1(B), R2(B), W2(B), where Ri and Wi denote the read and write operations of transaction Ti. Draw the precedence graph of S, determine whether S is conflict serializable and, if so, give an equivalent serial schedule.
answer_html:
To analyze schedule $S$, we identify all pairs of conflicting operations (operations by different transactions on the same data item where at least one is a write):

  • Conflicts on Data Item A: $R_1(A) < W_2(A)$, $W_1(A) < R_2(A)$, and $W_1(A) < W_2(A)$ all establish precedence edge $T_1 \to T_2$.
  • Conflicts on Data Item B: $R_1(B) < W_2(B)$, $W_1(B) < R_2(B)$, and $W_1(B) < W_2(B)$ also establish edge $T_1 \to T_2$.

Graph Analysis: In a precedence graph, a directed edge $T_i \to T_j$ indicates that $T_i$ executes a conflicting operation before $T_j$. Here, all conflicting pairs direct from $T_1$ to $T_2$ with zero reverse edges.

Serializability: Because the precedence graph contains no directed cycles (strictly acyclic), schedule $S$ is conflict serializable.

Equivalent Serial Schedule: Topological ordering gives $\langle T_1, T_2 \rangle$ ($T_1$ followed by $T_2$).
simplified_html: Every conflict on both items A and B has T1 running before T2. Since the arrow goes only one way (T1 → T2) with no loop, the schedule is conflict serializable and equivalent to running all of T1, then all of T2.

title: Explain log-based recovery with the deferred database modification and immediate database modification techniques.
answer_html:
Log-based recovery uses a write-ahead log (WAL) on stable storage to restore database consistency after crashes:

  • Deferred Database Modification: All write operations update only the log buffer in memory; the actual database on disk is modified only after the transaction commits.
    Recovery Policy: Since uncommitted updates are never written to disk, an UNDO is never required (NO-UNDO/REDO algorithm). During crash recovery, the DBMS only REDOes transactions whose log contains both <T start> and <T commit>.
  • Immediate Database Modification: Database updates can be written to disk while the transaction is still active, before committing (following WAL rules).
    Recovery Policy: Requires both UNDO and REDO (UNDO/REDO algorithm). Uncommitted transactions that modified disk blocks must be UNDONE, while committed transactions must be REDONE to guarantee durability.
simplified_html: Deferred modification: Don't touch disk until commit. If crash occurs, no undo needed, only redo committed ones. Immediate modification: Changes hit disk anytime. If crash occurs, undo uncommitted transactions and redo committed ones.

title: Explain dense and sparse indexes with an example. Which of the two requires less storage space and why?
answer_html:
Indexes accelerate search key lookups by mapping keys to disk block locations:

  • Dense Index: An index record appears for every search-key value in the data file. For duplicate keys, it points to the first record or a list of records. Fast lookups, but large index footprint.
    Example: An employee table with 10,000 records has 10,000 entries in its dense index.
  • Sparse Index: An index record appears for only some search-key values (typically one anchor key per disk block). Requires data records to be physically sorted by search key.
    Example: 10,000 records stored across 100 blocks require only 100 entries in a sparse index.
  • Storage Comparison: A sparse index requires significantly less storage space because it contains far fewer entries, allowing it to remain memory-resident and reducing I/O operations.
simplified_html: A dense index has a bookmark for every single page. A sparse index has a bookmark only for chapter beginnings. The sparse index uses much less storage space because it stores far fewer pointers.

title: Explain the unrepeatable read and phantom read problems of concurrent transactions with an example for each.
answer_html:
These two read anomalies occur under relaxed SQL isolation levels:

  • Unrepeatable (Fuzzy) Read: Transaction $T_1$ reads a specific row. Concurrently, transaction $T_2$ modifies or deletes that row and commits. When $T_1$ re-reads the exact same row, it discovers that the values have changed or the row disappeared.
    Example: $T_1$ reads employee John's salary as ₹50,000. $T_2$ updates John's salary to ₹60,000 and commits. $T_1$ re-reads John's record and finds ₹60,000, violating read repeatability.
  • Phantom Read: Transaction $T_1$ reads a set of rows satisfying a search predicate. Concurrently, transaction $T_2$ inserts a new row matching that predicate and commits. When $T_1$ re-executes the query, a new 'phantom' row appears.
    Example: $T_1$ runs SELECT count(*) WHERE dept='IT' (gets 5). $T_2$ inserts a new IT employee and commits. $T_1$ re-runs the count and gets 6.
simplified_html: Unrepeatable read: A value inside an existing row changes between two reads. Phantom read: Brand new rows appear or vanish from a query range between two reads because another transaction inserted them.

title: Distinguish between serial and non-serial schedules. Define conflict serializability and explain why a DBMS needs serializable schedules.
answer_html:
A schedule defines the chronological execution sequence of operations across concurrent transactions.

1. Serial vs. Non-Serial Schedules:

FeatureSerial ScheduleNon-Serial (Interleaved) Schedule
Execution OrderOperations of each transaction execute consecutively without interleaving.Operations of multiple transactions interleave concurrently.
Throughput & CPUPoor CPU and I/O resource utilization; waiting transactions block everything.High throughput and optimal resource utilization during I/O stalls.
ConsistencyAlways preserves consistency automatically without concurrency control.Can lead to anomalies (lost updates, dirty reads) unless serialized.
Response TimeHigh turnaround time for long transactions.Significantly reduced latency for short transactions.

2. Conflict Serializability:

A non-serial schedule $S$ is conflict serializable if it can be transformed into an equivalent serial schedule by a sequence of swaps of non-conflicting adjacent operations. Two operations conflict if they are issued by different transactions, operate on the same data item, and at least one is a write operation ($R_i(X)-W_j(X)$, $W_i(X)-R_j(X)$, or $W_i(X)-W_j(X)$).

A schedule is conflict serializable if and only if its precedence graph (conflict graph) contains no directed cycles.

3. Why a DBMS Needs Serializable Schedules:

  • Guaranteed Correctness: Since any serial execution preserves database consistency, a serializable concurrent schedule guarantees that the final state is mathematically correct.
  • Concurrency without Inconsistency: Allows the DBMS to maximize hardware parallelism, multi-core CPU throughput, and disk I/O overlap while completely eliminating race conditions and isolation anomalies.
  • ACID Isolation Invariant: Commercial database engines mandate serializability to fulfill the SQL standard Isolation requirement without forcing transactions to run strictly one at a time.
simplified_html: A serial schedule runs tasks one-by-one like a single-lane queue: completely safe, but dreadfully slow. A non-serial schedule runs tasks in parallel like a multi-lane highway: fast, but cars can crash into each other. A schedule is conflict serializable if its parallel execution produces the exact same end result as a safe single-lane queue without any crashes.

title: Explain recoverable, non-recoverable and cascadeless schedules and cascading rollback, giving a short example schedule for each.
answer_html:
Transaction recovery properties define how concurrent schedules behave when uncommitted dependencies encounter unexpected failures or aborts:

1. Non-Recoverable Schedule:

Occurs when transaction $T_2$ reads a data item modified by uncommitted transaction $T_1$, and $T_2$ commits before $T_1$. If $T_1$ subsequently aborts, $T_2$ has committed dirty data that cannot be rolled back without violating the Durability property of ACID.

Example: $S_1: W_1(A), R_2(A), Commit(T_2), Abort(T_1)$. Once $T_2$ commits, its results are permanently written to disk, leaving the database in an unrecoverable corrupted state.

2. Recoverable Schedule:

A schedule is recoverable if, whenever transaction $T_2$ reads a data item written by transaction $T_1$, the commit operation of $T_1$ precedes the commit operation of $T_2$ ($Commit(T_1) < Commit(T_2)$).

Example: $S_2: W_1(A), R_2(A), Commit(T_1), Commit(T_2)$. If $T_1$ aborts instead, $T_2$ has not yet committed and can be safely aborted too.

3. Cascading Rollback:

A phenomenon where the failure and rollback of a single transaction triggers a chain reaction of aborts across multiple dependent, uncommitted transactions that read its dirty uncommitted updates.

Example: $S_3: W_1(A), R_2(A), W_2(B), R_3(B), Abort(T_1)$. Because $T_1$ aborts, $T_2$ must abort, which in turn forces $T_3$ to abort, squandering significant CPU and disk I/O work.

4. Cascadeless Schedule:

A schedule is cascadeless (avoids cascading aborts) if every transaction reads only values written by already committed transactions ($Read_j(X)$ is delayed until after $Commit(T_i)$).

Example: $S_4: W_1(A), Commit(T_1), R_2(A), Commit(T_2)$. Since $T_2$ only reads after $T_1$ commits, an abort of $T_1$ can never affect $T_2$. Every cascadeless schedule is strictly recoverable.

Containment Hierarchy: The classes of schedules satisfy the strict inclusion relation: $\text{Strict Schedules} \subset \text{Cascadeless Schedules} \subset \text{Recoverable Schedules} \subset \text{All Possible Schedules}$. Commercial database engines enforce cascadelessness or strictness to maintain continuous system throughput.
simplified_html: Non-recoverable: You commit work based on someone else's uncommitted notes, and they delete their draft (disaster). Recoverable: You wait for them to submit before you submit. Cascading rollback: One person's mistake forces ten other people to scrap their work. Cascadeless: Nobody is allowed to read a note until it is officially submitted and approved.

title: Explain how deadlocks are detected using a wait-for graph, and explain the deadlock recovery schemes: victim selection, rollback and the avoidance of starvation.
answer_html:
A deadlock occurs in lock-based concurrency control when transactions enter circular wait states for held locks.

1. Deadlock Detection via Wait-For Graph (WFG):

A Wait-For Graph is a directed graph $G = (V, E)$ maintained dynamically by the lock manager where vertices $V$ represent active transactions and directed edge $T_i \to T_j$ indicates that $T_i$ is suspended waiting for a lock currently held by $T_j$. When a lock request cannot be granted, an edge is added; when a lock is released, corresponding edges are deleted.

The lock manager invokes cycle-detection algorithms (e.g., Depth-First Search or Tarjan's strongly connected components algorithm) at scheduled intervals. A deadlock exists if and only if the WFG contains a directed cycle.

2. Deadlock Recovery Schemes:

  • Victim Selection: When a cycle is detected, the DBMS chooses one transaction in the cycle to abort. The selection minimizes overall rollback overhead based on criteria such as elapsed execution time, remaining queries, number of modified rows, and number of cascading rollbacks prevented.
  • Rollback Policy:
    • Total Rollback: Abort the victim completely and restart it from the very beginning.
    • Partial Rollback: Roll back the victim only to an intermediate savepoint sufficient to release the contested lock and break the graph cycle, saving prior computational work.
  • Avoidance of Starvation: If victim selection always chooses the youngest transaction or the one with the fewest updates, that transaction could repeatedly be aborted and starved from ever finishing. To prevent starvation, the DBMS associates an abort count with each transaction; each abort increments its priority so an older transaction is never starved indefinitely.
simplified_html: The DBMS draws arrows between transactions showing who is waiting for whom. If the arrows form a closed circle, it is a deadlock. To break it: (1) Pick a 'victim' transaction that is cheap to abort, (2) Roll it back (partially or totally) to release its locks, and (3) Ensure the same transaction isn't picked repeatedly so it doesn't starve forever.

title: Explain shared (S) and exclusive (X) locks along with the lock compatibility matrix, and describe the basic two-phase locking protocol, including its growing phase, shrinking phase and lock point.
answer_html:
Lock-based concurrency control protocols restrict concurrent data access using complementary lock modes and acquisition phases:

1. Shared (S) and Exclusive (X) Locks:

  • Shared Lock ($S$): Read-only lock mode. If a transaction holds a shared lock on data item $Q$, other concurrent transactions can also acquire shared locks on $Q$ ($S-S$ is compatible). No writes are permitted.
  • Exclusive Lock ($X$): Read-write lock mode. Only one transaction can hold an exclusive lock on $Q$ at any given moment ($X-S$ and $X-X$ are strictly incompatible).

Lock Compatibility Matrix:

Requested \ HeldShared ($S$)Exclusive ($X$)
Shared ($S$)Compatible (True)Incompatible (False)
Exclusive ($X$)Incompatible (False)Incompatible (False)

2. Two-Phase Locking (2PL) Protocol:

The basic 2PL protocol guarantees conflict serializability by requiring every transaction to separate its lock operations into two distinct, non-overlapping phases:

  • Phase 1: Growing (Expanding) Phase: The transaction acquires new locks as needed and may upgrade locks ($S \to X$). It cannot release any lock under any circumstances.
  • Lock Point: The exact instant when the transaction acquires its final lock (reaches peak lock count). The chronological order of lock points across transactions dictates their exact conflict serialization order.
  • Phase 2: Shrinking (Contracting) Phase: The transaction releases held locks and may downgrade locks ($X \to S$). It cannot acquire any new locks once this phase begins.

Serializability Guarantee: Because transactions never acquire new locks after releasing an earlier lock, no circular data item dependencies can be created, proving that 2PL guarantees conflict serializability.
simplified_html: A Shared lock is like reading a public book (everyone can read). An Exclusive lock is like writing in your private diary (only one person allowed). In 2PL, you gather all keys during the growing phase until your 'lock point', and once you return even one key (shrinking phase), you can never pick up another key again.

title: Compare strict and rigorous two-phase locking with the help of an example, and state the benefits of each.
answer_html:
Strict 2PL and Rigorous 2PL are specialized variants of the Two-Phase Locking protocol that enforce stronger guarantees than basic 2PL.

1. Strict Two-Phase Locking (Strict 2PL):

  • Rule: In addition to basic 2PL rules, a transaction must hold all its exclusive ($X$) locks until it terminates (commits or aborts). Shared ($S$) locks can be released during the shrinking phase before commit.
  • Benefits: Guarantees recoverable and cascadeless schedules (prevents dirty reads), simplifying transaction rollback without cascading aborts. Allows concurrent reads to proceed earlier when shared locks are released.

2. Rigorous Two-Phase Locking (Rigorous 2PL):

  • Rule: A transaction must hold all locks (both Shared $S$ and Exclusive $X$) until it terminates (commits or aborts). The shrinking phase collapses to the commit/abort point.
  • Benefits: Guarantees strict serializability. Transactions can be serialized in the exact order in which they commit, making schedule analysis and replication coordination straightforward.

3. Comparative Example Schedule:

Consider transaction $T_1$ needing to read $A$ and update $B$, and transaction $T_2$ needing to read $A$:

  • Under Strict 2PL: $T_1$ acquires $S(A)$ and $X(B)$. After reading $A$, $T_1$ can release $S(A)$ early. $T_2$ can immediately acquire $S(A)$ and read $A$ before $T_1$ commits. However, $T_1$ retains $X(B)$ until commit.
  • Under Rigorous 2PL: $T_1$ acquires $S(A)$ and $X(B)$. $T_1$ cannot release $S(A)$ until it commits. $T_2$ must wait if it needs an exclusive lock, ensuring strict chronological locking isolation.
DimensionStrict 2PLRigorous 2PL
X-locks held untilCommit / AbortCommit / Abort
S-locks held untilCan release in shrinking phaseCommit / Abort
Concurrency LevelHigher (early S-lock release)Lower (locks held longer)
Commit OrderingMay differ from lock pointIdentical to commit order
simplified_html: Under Strict 2PL, you keep private writing pens ($X$-locks) until you finish, but you can return reading glasses ($S$-locks) early. Under Rigorous 2PL, you return nothing until you officially check out (commit). Rigorous is simpler and orders transactions by checkout time, but Strict allows more concurrency.

title: Explain the architecture of a data warehouse (data sources, staging area, warehouse and presentation layer), describe the ETL process and state the role of data marts.
answer_html:
A Data Warehouse (DW) is a subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant, and non-volatile collection of corporate data structured for management decision-support analysis.

1. Architectural Layers:

  • Data Sources: Operational transactional databases (OLTP), enterprise ERP and CRM systems, flat log files, web clickstreams, and third-party APIs.
  • Staging Area: An intermediate holding and processing area where incoming data is extracted, sanitized, validated, and normalized before warehouse insertion, isolating production OLTP systems from query load.
  • Warehouse (Enterprise Storage): The central repository storing integrated historical and atomic granular data organized according to enterprise-wide relational or dimensional data models.
  • Presentation Layer: Front-end client applications providing reporting dashboards, OLAP multidimensional cubes, data visualization, and predictive data mining tools.
  • Metadata Repository: Maintains administrative schemas, ETL business rules, transformation lineage, and indexing definitions, serving as the system directory across all warehouse components.

2. The ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) Process:

  • Extract: Captures changed data (CDC) from heterogeneous relational databases, legacy systems, and unstructured files without interrupting live transaction processing.
  • Transform: Performs critical data cleansing (handling null values and duplicates), standardizing disparate formats (e.g., converting dates to ISO standard, harmonizing currency codes), joining reference data, and generating artificial surrogate primary keys.
  • Load: Executes bulk insertions of curated records into the target warehouse fact and dimension tables during scheduled batch loading windows.

3. Role of Data Marts:

A data mart is a departmental, highly focused subset of the warehouse customized for specific business units (such as Marketing, Finance, or Logistics). By structuring data into dedicated star or snowflake schemas, data marts deliver accelerated query performance, tighter security isolation, and tailored analytics without traversing the massive enterprise warehouse.
simplified_html: Data warehousing works like a restaurant: raw ingredients arrive from farms (Data Sources), get washed and chopped in the kitchen (Staging/ETL), stored in cold storage (Enterprise DW), and served as tailored dishes at customer tables (Data Marts & BI Dashboards).

title: Why is two-phase locking (mostly strict 2PL) used in commercial DBMSs? Show with an example schedule that it can still cause deadlock, and write its other drawbacks.
answer_html:
Commercial database engines (such as Oracle, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server) overwhelmingly implement Strict Two-Phase Locking (Strict 2PL) as their primary concurrency control protocol.

1. Why Commercial DBMSs Adopt Strict 2PL:

  • Guarantees Serializability: Like basic 2PL, it mathematically guarantees that all concurrent interleaved schedules are conflict serializable.
  • Eliminates Cascading Aborts: By holding exclusive ($X$) locks until commit, transactions never write data that others read uncommitted; schedules are strictly cascadeless and recoverable.
  • Simple Crash Recovery: Transaction rollback requires only undoing before-images without inspecting or aborting other transactions.

2. Deadlock Schedule Example under Strict 2PL:

Strict 2PL does not prevent deadlocks. Consider two transactions $T_1$ and $T_2$ accessing data items $A$ and $B$:

  • $T_1$ acquires $X(A)$ and writes to $A$.
  • $T_2$ acquires $X(B)$ and writes to $B$.
  • $T_1$ requests $X(B)$: since $T_2$ holds $X(B)$ until commit, $T_1$ must wait for $T_2$.
  • $T_2$ requests $X(A)$: since $T_1$ holds $X(A)$ until commit, $T_2$ must wait for $T_1$.

Both transactions hold resources while waiting for each other ($T_1 \to T_2 \to T_1$), creating a mutual deadlock that requires DBMS intervention.

3. Drawbacks of Two-Phase Locking:

  • Deadlock Overhead: Systems must dedicate CPU cycles to maintain wait-for graphs, run cycle-detection routines, and abort/restart victims.
  • Reduced Concurrency & Lock Convoying: Long-running write transactions holding exclusive locks stall all subsequent readers and writers, degrading multi-user throughput.
  • Lock Maintenance Cost: Allocating, updating, and hashing lock table entries adds memory consumption and lock manager processing latency.
  • Phantom Anomalies: Tuple-level 2PL cannot stop phantom inserts into range queries unless expensive predicate/index-range locking is used.
simplified_html: Strict 2PL is popular because it guarantees safety and clean rollbacks without domino-effect cancellations. However, it can still cause deadlocks: if T1 locks A waiting for B, and T2 locks B waiting for A, they freeze. Its other downsides are lower concurrency, lock table memory overhead, and lock queues.

title: Explain the deadlock prevention schemes Wait-Die and Wound-Wait with examples.
answer_html:
Deadlock prevention protocols use transaction timestamps to decide whether a requesting transaction should wait or abort when a resource conflict occurs. Monotonic timestamp $TS(T_i)$ is assigned when transaction $T_i$ begins (smaller timestamp implies older transaction).

Suppose transaction $T_i$ requests a lock held by transaction $T_j$:

1. Wait-Die Scheme (Non-Preemptive):

  • Older requests from Younger ($TS(T_i) < TS(T_j)$): $T_i$ is allowed to wait.
  • Younger requests from Older ($TS(T_i) > TS(T_j)$): $T_i$ dies (aborts) and restarts with its original timestamp.
  • Rule Summary: 'Old waits, young dies.' Locks are never preemptively stolen.
  • Example: Let $TS(T_1)=10$ (older) and $TS(T_2)=20$ (younger). If $T_1$ requests a lock held by $T_2$, $T_1$ waits. If $T_2$ requests a lock held by $T_1$, $T_2$ dies and restarts.

2. Wound-Wait Scheme (Preemptive):

  • Older requests from Younger ($TS(T_i) < TS(T_j)$): $T_i$ wounds $T_j$; $T_j$ is preempted, aborted, and rolls back, releasing its lock to $T_i$. $T_j$ restarts with its original timestamp.
  • Younger requests from Older ($TS(T_i) > TS(T_j)$): $T_i$ is allowed to wait.
  • Rule Summary: 'Old wounds, young waits.' Younger transactions are preempted by older ones.
  • Example: With $TS(T_1)=10$ and $TS(T_2)=20$, if $T_1$ requests a lock held by $T_2$, $T_1$ preempts ($T_2$ is aborted). If $T_2$ requests a lock held by $T_1$, $T_2$ waits.

3. Key Comparison:

MetricWait-DieWound-Wait
PreemptionNon-preemptivePreemptive
Number of AbortsHigh (young transactions die repeatedly)Fewer aborts; locks granted quickly to old
StarvationAvoided (retains original timestamp)Avoided (retains original timestamp)

Starvation Freedom Guarantee: In both schemes, when an aborted transaction restarts, it keeps its original starting timestamp. Thus, as time passes, the transaction becomes progressively older relative to new transactions, guaranteeing that it eventually becomes the oldest active transaction and runs to completion without ever dying again.
simplified_html: Think of timestamps as age (older has priority). In Wait-Die: seniors are patient and wait for juniors, but if a junior asks a senior, the junior dies. In Wound-Wait: seniors don't wait; they wound and kick out juniors, while juniors patiently wait for seniors. Both prevent deadlock cycles.

title: Construct a B+ tree in which every node can hold at most 3 keys (a maximum of 4 child pointers) by inserting the keys 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 and 70 in the given order. Show the tree after every node split and state two advantages of a B+ tree over a B-tree.
answer_html:
Node Specification: Max keys $M = 3$, maximum child pointers $P = 4$. A node splits when the number of keys reaches 4.

Step-by-Step Construction:

  • Insert 10, 20, 30: All fit in the single root leaf node: [10, 20, 30].
  • Insert 40 (Split 1): Node overflows to [10, 20, 30, 40]. In a B+ tree leaf split, the middle key (index $\lceil 4/2 \rceil = 2$, key 30) is copied up to the parent. Left leaf keeps [10, 20], right leaf keeps [30, 40] with a leaf sibling pointer. New root becomes [30].
  • Insert 50: Placed into right leaf: [30, 40, 50]. Tree valid.
  • Insert 60 (Split 2): Right leaf overflows to [30, 40, 50, 60]. Leaf splits: left leaf retains [30, 40], right leaf gets [50, 60], and key 50 is copied up to root. Root now contains keys [30, 50].
  • Insert 70: Placed into rightmost leaf: [50, 60, 70]. Node is full but does not exceed 3 keys.

Two Distinct Advantages of a B+ Tree over a Standard B-Tree:

  • Extremely Fast Sequential Range Queries: In a B+ tree, all leaf nodes are linked into a continuous linked list. Range queries execute by jumping to the start key via root search and simply scanning linearly across leaf sibling pointers, completely avoiding expensive in-order tree traversals required by B-trees.
  • Higher Fanout and Lower Tree Height: Internal nodes in a B+ tree store only search keys and child pointers without actual data records. Consequently, each fixed-size disk page fits significantly more branch pointers (higher fanout), making the tree shallower and drastically reducing the number of disk I/O operations required for lookups.
simplified_html: As numbers are inserted, leaves split whenever they exceed 3 keys, pushing middle values up to form the root [30, 50]. The final leaves are [10, 20] → [30, 40] → [50, 60, 70], chained together like a train. B+ trees beat B-trees because leaves form a linked list for easy range scanning, and internal nodes fit more keys per disk page.

title: A static hash file uses the hash function h(k) = k mod 5. Each bucket holds at most 2 records and overflow is handled by chaining. Insert the keys 5, 12, 21, 9, 17, 14, 8, 33, 22 and 7 in the given order and show the final contents of each bucket. Also explain how extendible hashing avoids long overflow chains. 5 Sr. No. Question Marks 120 A retail chain wants to analyse its sales by store, product and month. (i) Design a star schema with one fact table and suitable dimension tables. (ii) Explain the OLAP operations roll -up, drill-down and slice with an example from this schema. (iii) Analyse how the OLAP workload on this warehouse differs from the OLTP workload of the stores' billing systems.
answer_html:
Part 1: Static Hashing ($h(k) = k \bmod 5$, Bucket Capacity = 2, Chaining):

  • $k=5: 5 \bmod 5 = 0 \to$ Bucket 0: [5]
  • $k=12: 12 \bmod 5 = 2 \to$ Bucket 2: [12]
  • $k=21: 21 \bmod 5 = 1 \to$ Bucket 1: [21]
  • $k=9: 9 \bmod 5 = 4 \to$ Bucket 4: [9]
  • $k=17: 17 \bmod 5 = 2 \to$ Bucket 2: [12, 17] (Full)
  • $k=14: 14 \bmod 5 = 4 \to$ Bucket 4: [9, 14] (Full)
  • $k=8: 8 \bmod 5 = 3 \to$ Bucket 3: [8]
  • $k=33: 33 \bmod 5 = 3 \to$ Bucket 3: [8, 33] (Full)
  • $k=22: 22 \bmod 5 = 2 \to$ Bucket 2 overflows $\to$ Chained Overflow Block: [22]
  • $k=7: 7 \bmod 5 = 2 \to$ Bucket 2 overflow chain: [22, 7]

Final Bucket Contents: Bucket 0: [5]; Bucket 1: [21]; Bucket 2: Primary [12, 17] $\to$ Chained Overflow [22, 7]; Bucket 3: [8, 33]; Bucket 4: [9, 14].

How Extendible Hashing Avoids Long Chains: Extendible hashing uses a dynamic directory with global and local depth. When a bucket overflows, only that specific bucket splits, doubling its local depth. If local depth exceeds global depth, the directory doubles. Records are redistributed using additional hash bits, preventing sequential linear overflow search degradation.

Part 2: Retail Star Schema & OLAP Workload:

  • Star Schema Design: Central fact table Sales_Fact with measures (quantity_sold, total_revenue) and foreign keys (store_id, product_id, time_id), surrounded by dimension tables Store_Dim (location, city), Product_Dim (category, brand), and Time_Dim (day, month, quarter, year).
  • OLAP Operations:
    • Roll-up: Aggregates sales from Month to Year level.
    • Drill-down: De-aggregates sales from Product Category down to individual Item.
    • Slice: Filters sales for a single store (e.g., store_id = 'Store_101').
  • OLAP vs. OLTP Workload: Store billing (OLTP) executes frequent, short, write-intensive ACID transactions with normalized schemas. The warehouse (OLAP) executes long-running, read-mostly, complex multi-table analytical aggregations over millions of denormalized historical records.
simplified_html: Keys are mapped to buckets 0-4 using $k \bmod 5$. When bucket 2 fills with [12, 17], keys 22 and 7 spill into a chained overflow block. Extendible hashing eliminates overflow chains by splitting buckets dynamically. For retail analytics, a central Sales Fact table is surrounded by Store, Product, and Time dimensions; OLAP lets managers zoom out (roll-up) or zoom in (drill-down) on revenues.

title: Differentiate between fragmentation and replication in a distributed database.
answer_html:
The core differences between fragmentation and replication in distributed databases are:

  • Fragmentation: Divides a logical relation into non-overlapping sub-relations (horizontal rows, vertical columns, or hybrid) distributed across different sites without data duplication.
  • Replication: Stores redundant full copies of a relation or fragment at two or more geographically distributed network sites to enhance availability and read locality.
simplified_html: Fragmentation is slicing a pizza so each person gets a different slice (splitting data without copies). Replication is photocopying the exact same document so everyone has their own identical copy.

title: State any two advantages and one drawback of data replication in a distributed database.
answer_html:
Data replication in distributed databases offers significant benefits and distinct trade-offs:

  • Advantage 1 (High Availability): If a node holding data crashes, queries are transparently serviced by surviving replicas without downtime.
  • Advantage 2 (Fast Read Performance): Read operations execute locally at the nearest replica site, eliminating wide-area network latency.
  • Drawback (Update Overhead): Every write must be synchronized across all replicas, requiring distributed consensus protocols that increase write latency.
simplified_html: Pros: (1) If one server dies, backups keep running seamlessly; (2) Local servers answer reads lightning fast. Con: Updating data is slow because changes must be sent and confirmed across every single backup node.

title: Define an index in MongoDB and state why it is used.
answer_html:
An index in MongoDB is a specialized auxiliary data structure (implemented as a B-tree) that stores a small portion of a collection's document fields in an easily traversable, sorted order.

Why it is used:

  • Query Acceleration: Avoids expensive full collection scans (COLLSCAN) by allowing the query engine to rapidly locate documents (IXSCAN).
  • Efficient Sorting: Fulfills sorted queries directly from the index order without memory-intensive sort operations.
simplified_html: Just like a book index lets you jump straight to page 120 instead of reading the entire book word-by-word, a MongoDB index stores sorted field pointers so the database finds documents instantly.

title: What is the purpose of the _id field in a MongoDB document?
answer_html:
The _id field serves as the mandatory primary key for every document in a MongoDB collection, uniquely identifying it within that collection.

  • Default Generation: If omitted during insertion, MongoDB automatically populates _id with a unique 12-byte ObjectId (composed of timestamp, machine identifier, process ID, and incrementing counter).
  • Unique Index: MongoDB automatically builds and maintains a unique index on _id, ensuring fast document lookups and preventing duplicate keys.
simplified_html: The _id field is like a Social Security Number or Roll Number for each MongoDB document. It uniquely identifies the record and automatically gets a built-in search index so you can find it instantly.

title: State the CAP theorem and name its three properties.
answer_html:
Brewer's CAP Theorem states that any distributed data store can simultaneously guarantee at most two out of three properties in the presence of network partitions.

Its three core properties are:

  • Consistency (C): Every read receives the most recent write or an error.
  • Availability (A): Every non-failing node returns a non-error response for every request (without guaranteeing latest data).
  • Partition Tolerance (P): The system continues to operate despite arbitrary network message losses or node network isolations.
simplified_html: The CAP theorem says you can't have it all in a distributed network. When cables snap (Partition), you must choose: either freeze until data synchronizes (Consistency) or keep answering with possibly stale data (Availability).

title: What is a replica set in MongoDB?
answer_html:
A replica set in MongoDB is a cluster of mongod processes that maintain identical data copies to provide high availability and automatic failover.

  • Primary Node: Exactly one primary receives all write operations, recording modifications in its replication operation log (oplog).
  • Secondary Nodes: Multiple secondaries continuously replicate the primary's oplog and apply operations asynchronously. If the primary fails, secondaries elect a new primary via consensus.
simplified_html: A replica set is a team of database servers. One is the captain (Primary) that handles all changes, while the others (Secondaries) copy everything. If the captain drops, the team votes in a new captain within seconds.

title: Define sharding and state why it is used in MongoDB.
answer_html:
Sharding is a method for distributing data horizontally across multiple machines or clusters using a designated partition field known as a shard key.

Why it is used in MongoDB:

  • Horizontal Scalability (Scale-Out): Overcomes the hardware limits (RAM, CPU, disk I/O) of a single server by adding affordable commodity servers.
  • Throughput Distribution: Partitions massive data sets and splits high-volume read/write query loads across independent shard servers.
simplified_html: Sharding is horizontal scaling: when a single database server gets too full or too slow to handle traffic, you split your collection into pieces (shards) across multiple computers so work is divided evenly.

title: Explain the main types of NoSQL databases and give one example product for each type.
answer_html:
NoSQL databases diverge from relational models by adopting non-tabular, flexible storage architectures:

  • Key-Value Store: Stores data as associative arrays of unique keys paired with arbitrary binary values. Highly optimized for simple $O(1)$ lookups and session caches.
    Example: Redis, Amazon DynamoDB.
  • Document-Oriented Database: Stores semi-structured data as self-describing BSON/JSON documents with nested objects and arrays, eliminating fixed relational schemas.
    Example: MongoDB, Couchbase.
  • Column-Family (Wide-Column) Store: Organizes data into columns grouped into column families rather than rows, enabling high compression and massive analytical read throughput.
    Example: Apache Cassandra, Apache HBase.
  • Graph Database: Represents data as nodes (entities) and edges (explicit relationships) with key-value properties, designed for complex network traversals without recursive relational joins.
    Example: Neo4j, Amazon Neptune.
simplified_html: NoSQL comes in four flavors: Key-Value (Redis) like a locker with labeled keys; Document (MongoDB) like filing cabinets of JSON forms; Wide-Column (Cassandra) storing huge data by column instead of row; and Graph (Neo4j) connecting people like friends on Facebook.

title: Describe how data is organised in MongoDB into databases, collections and documents, with an example.
answer_html:
MongoDB organizes data hierarchically into three structural levels:

  • Database: The outermost container that manages a physical set of files on disk. A single MongoDB instance can host multiple independent databases (e.g., universityDB).
  • Collection: A group of related documents housed inside a database, analogous to a relational table. However, collections are schema-free: documents in a collection do not need identical fields.
